# The Man on South Street

I met him on South Street, where the salt air hangs thick over the docks and the gulls wheel low against a colorless sky. He was a tall man, unusually so, with a nervous energy that seemed to run just beneath his skin like a current. But it was his eyes that arrested me—a striking, luminous green, the color of deep water catching light, and yet fixed on something impossibly distant. He looked at me, and through me, all at once. There was a hollowness in his gaze, the vivid impression of a man who had traveled far beyond the ordinary boundaries of experience and had never quite found his way back.

We drifted, somehow, into a bar along the waterfront. Inside, a piano played softly in the corner, its melody threading through the smoke and murmur of low conversation. The tune was "Stamboul Nights," and beneath it, again and again, rose the recurring refrain—"Stamboul Rose"—winding dreamlike through the dim room, so that the whole scene seemed suspended somewhere between memory and sleep. The notes lingered, dissolved, and returned, and the man's restless fingers tapped against the bar in time with them.

"You must remind me," he said suddenly, leaning close. His voice carried a strange urgency. "My ship—the S.S. *Ala*—she sails at three. You mustn't let me forget." He gripped the edge of the counter as though steadying himself against some invisible pitch and roll. "I can no longer keep track of the hours. Time slips from me. I cannot hold it."

He must have seen the question forming on my face, for he began, unprompted, to explain. He had been a whaler once, he told me, in the far northern seas. Something had happened to him up there, in the endless Arctic light and the crushing dark that followed—the harsh, indifferent cold had done something to him, unmoored him from the natural rhythm of things. The long white days that never ended, the nights that swallowed weeks whole; they had destroyed his sense of time entirely and left him, ever after, unable to function as other men did.

And then he spoke of the wandering years that came afterward. He had labored in Panama, sweating in the shadow of the great canal. He had sold kitchenware across the dusty roads of Yucatan, moving from village to village, and had traveled the length of the coast with no purpose he could name. As he spoke, the images seemed to rise from him like heat: ruined cities standing silent in the jungle, their stones reclaimed by vine and root; the black, desolate slopes of volcanic country, ashen and lifeless beneath a burning sky. He conjured a whole geography of desolation, one landscape bleeding into the next, until I could no longer tell whether he described the world he had seen or the ruined country that lay within him.

And through it all, the piano played on—*Stamboul Rose, Stamboul Rose*—and the man's green eyes stared past me toward the sea.

# Phosphor Reef

*after Hart Crane*

I met a man in a Water Street cellar
where the fog came in on the soles of drowned men—
his eyes were two green fires banked in wet coal,
*green glass, or the neon spilling salt through the pane?*

He tipped his glass. The rum went down like tide.
*O Valparaiso—dreams drag the anchor down!*
the nickel pianola stammered, coughing brine,
its keys the teeth of something that had drowned.

"Seen the doldrums flatten like a griddle—
seen Saint Elmo crawl the yards in blue—"
his hands were charts, all longitude and tremble,
the knuckles ports he swore he'd sailed clean through.

*the phosphor wakes—the phosphor wakes and wheels—*

Somewhere a bell-buoy tolled inside his throat.
He couldn't stop. The tropics burned his talk.
Typhoons unspooled from him like slackened rope
and every word slid seaward off the dock.

"I lost the year in Java—found it grinning
in a girl's teeth, gone by the morning gun—"
His green eyes turned. They were not looking at me.
They stared clean past the wall into the sun

that sank forever in some other ocean.
*O Stamboul—no—O anywhere at all—*
The record skipped. The dawn came grey as ashes.
I left him talking to the rum-stained wall.

And climbing up to daybreak on the cobbles
I heard the harbor loose its ghostly fleet—

*Thermopylae, Ariel, running the trades—
Flying Cloud shaking her acres of sail—
Sea Witch, Nightingale, dropping Sandy Hook—
Cutty Sark hull-down in the green of a gale—*

—their canvas thundering somewhere out past waking,
their green lamps burning low along the swell,
while down in the cellar, still, a drowned man's eyes
kept two small tides no morning could dispel.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about an encounter with a mysterious sailor whose stories drift through Panama, Yucatan, Popocatepetl, and the Arctic, with a hypnotic song echoing throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sailor's Song

He came ashore with salt-white hair,
his eyes like fathoms, deep and slow,
and sat beside me, unaware
of how his tales began to flow—

*"Oh, listen, listen,"* soft he sang,
*"the tide remembers where I've been..."*
and through his words the harbor rang
with distant shores I'd never seen.

In Panama the jungles breathed,
where two great oceans nearly kissed,
and vessels through the locks were sheathed
in emerald light and morning mist.

*"Oh, listen, listen,"* rose his tune,
*"the water carries every name..."*
and Yucatan beneath the moon
bloomed limestone-pale and green as flame—

where ancient stones the divers found
beneath the cenotes, cool and blue,
and silence made a holy sound
the drowning centuries once knew.

Then Popocatepetl loomed,
a smoking crown against the sky,
its ashen shoulders vast, perfumed
with sulfur where the eagles fly.

*"Oh, listen, listen,"* on he went,
*"the cold will call you north at last..."*
and Arctic light through silence bent
where glaciers held the frozen past.

He spoke of white unending days,
of ice that groaned like living things,
of compass-needles set ablaze
beneath the green auroral wings.

And when I turned to ask him how
a single life could hold such seas—
the bench was bare, the empty prow
of some far ship slid through the breeze.

But still, when fog rolls off the bay
and gulls trace circles overhead,
I hear him singing far away,
*"Oh, listen, listen,"*—soft as thread.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# The Nickel Piano at World's End

*

Somewhere the tide keeps its ledger—
each wave a coin, each coin a face
I owned once, or dreamed I did.

The piano eats another nickel.
Music limps out on wet feet.

*

"I've been," he says, and his glass
becomes a porthole—
                    *I've been to*
where the mountains wear salt
and the women speak in gulls—

or was that here? Was that
the mirror behind the bottles
throwing my own coast back at me?

*

The bartender polishes the same clean spot.
Round and round. A small ecstatic wound
in the mahogany.

Outside, the fog files its report.
Nothing to add. Nothing subtracted.

*

He remembers a ship. Or the idea
of leaving,
            which is lighter,
                            which travels farther
than any actual departure.

*I loved her in Lisbon.*
*I loved her in the next stool over.*
*I loved the loving, mostly—*
the piano agrees, drops a note
through the floorboards
into the harbor's dark museum.

*

Now the room tilts its long deck.
Now the stranger is a boy again
counting foreign money into someone's palm,
counting stars that turn out to be
the ceiling's water-stains,
constellations of a drunk cartographer.

*

"Buy me," he begins,
and forgets the object of the buying.
We all lean in. Even the fog leans in.

*

The nickel piano.
The wine like burning ink.
The doorway where the sea keeps
almost, almost
                    coming in—

and he lifts his glass to all of it:
to memory, that unreliable ferryman,
to the countries he invented
crossing this one dark
                        and salted
                                    room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
